Red Blue Chair

Rietveld’s armchair of square battens and two flat boards: a red back, a blue seat, and a black frame whose cut ends are painted yellow.

Source
Wikipedia: Red and Blue Chair
Creator
Gerrit Rietveld
Made
Designed 1917–1918; painted in its known colors in the early 1920s (about 1923 per MoMA)
Style
De Stijl (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Constructive, planar, iconic
Evidence
Inspected a photograph by Daderot of the copy in the Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln, labeled “Roodblauwe Stoel … G. A. van de Groenekan, Utrecht NL, 1918, lacquered wood” (Commons, 3222 × 4039 px, viewed at 1280 px). Many copies exist and they differ. The MoMA page returned 403 to the fetch tool; MoMA facts come from its catalogue text as shown in search results.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Wikipedia dates the design to 1917 and states that the chair was not painted in its distinct colors until the early 1920s, and that several versions are held in collections. Wikipedia.

MoMA dates its copy 1918–1923, painted wood, 86.7 × 66 × 83.8 cm, and states that the red, yellow, blue, and black scheme was applied around 1923. MoMA.

Observed

  • The back is a flat red board set at a steep slant; the seat is a flat dark blue board set at a shallower slant.
  • The frame is made of square black battens that cross each other and run past every joint.
  • Every cut end of a batten is painted yellow, which makes small yellow squares at the ends.
  • The armrests are flat black boards resting on the frame.
  • In this museum photograph the chair stands on a white plinth in front of a frosted window.

Why it belongs

The chair applies the painting rule to an object: lines become battens, planes become boards, and the joints are left visible as overlaps rather than hidden.

The yellow ends show how a primary can be used as a point accent that marks where a line ends.

Borrow

Mark the ends of lines or bars with a small square of a primary.

Let structural bars cross and overshoot, and keep flat panels in single colors.
